page_subtitle: Plain answers about what you own and what you have been offered.
meta_description: Help for Pennsylvania and Appalachian Basin mineral owners: ownership reports, heirship research, Marcellus lease offer review, and division order questions.
intro:
If someone has approached you about leasing your minerals, crossing your land, or signing a division order, you do not have to work out what it means on your own.

We are Certified Professional Landmen. We read the public record for a living. We can tell you what the record shows about your ownership, what a document in front of you actually says, and, just as importantly, what the record does not settle.
services_headline: What You Can Bring to Us

services.title: Mineral ownership reports
services.description: A written report of what the public record shows you own, how that interest came to you, and where the chain of title is unclear or incomplete.

services.title: Heirship and succession research
services.description: Tracing an interest through estates, probate and heirship when a relative's ownership was never formally passed down on paper.

services.title: Lease offer review
services.description: Checking an offer against the record: whether the tract described is the tract you own, whether the interest stated matches what the record shows, and which terms are worth asking about.

lease_packet.label: Lease Offers
lease_packet.headline: What Is in a Lease Offer
lease_packet.intro: A lease offer usually arrives as three documents. Here is what each one does and which terms to read first.

documents.title: The lease
documents.text: The printed form. It names the parties, grants the right to explore and produce, and sets the term and the royalty. Most offers today are paid-up leases, which means the bonus paid at signing covers the whole primary term and no yearly rentals follow.

documents.title: The exhibit or addendum
documents.text: This carries the legal description and the negotiated terms. It usually says that it controls wherever it conflicts with the printed form, so read it first.

documents.title: The memorandum of lease
documents.text: A short version recorded at the courthouse in place of the full lease. It gives public notice that the lease exists without putting the bonus and royalty into the public record.

terms.title: Acreage
terms.text: The bonus is paid per net mineral acre. The acreage stated in the lease and the interest you are credited with decide the size of the check.

terms.title: Primary term and option to extend
terms.text: The primary term is how long the company can hold the lease without drilling. An option lets the company add years for a set payment without coming back to you.

terms.title: Royalty
terms.text: Look at the fraction, and at whether the costs of processing and moving the gas are taken out before your share is calculated.

terms.title: Pooling
terms.text: This sets how large a unit your acreage can be combined into. Your share of unit production follows your share of the acreage in the unit.

terms.title: Shut-in clause
terms.text: This lets the company hold the lease with a small yearly payment while a well can produce but is not selling.

terms.title: Pugh clause
terms.text: This releases acreage, and sometimes depths, that are not in a producing unit when the primary term ends. Without one, a single well can hold the whole lease.

terms.title: Continuous operations
terms.text: This defines what activity keeps the lease alive after the primary term, and how long a gap between operations is allowed.

terms.title: Surface use and damages
terms.text: This covers what the company may build on the surface and what it pays for damage. Some leases bar surface operations entirely.

terms.title: Warranty of title
terms.text: This is whether you are promising that you own what the lease says you own.

terms.title: Preferential right
terms.text: Some leases give the company the right to match a later offer from a competitor before you can accept it.

terms.title: Indemnity
terms.text: This says who is responsible if the company's operations lead to a claim.

lease_packet.closing: We can check an offer against the record and explain what each clause does. For advice on whether to sign, talk to an oil and gas attorney.

faq.question: What does a landman actually do?
faq.answer: A landman works out who owns what, using the public record. In practice that means going through deeds, leases, wills, probate files and court records at the county courthouse, tracing an interest back through every transfer it has been through, and writing up what the record shows. Certified Professional Landman is the credential the American Association of Professional Landmen issues for that work.

faq.question: I inherited minerals and I am not sure what I own. Can you find out?
faq.answer: Usually, yes, and it is ordinary work for us. We trace the interest back through the deeds and the probate records and report what the record supports. Inherited interests often have gaps in them, where an estate was never settled or a transfer was never filed, sometimes several generations back and in a county nobody thought to look in. Those gaps are exactly what we go looking for.

faq.question: Can you tell me whether the offer I received is a fair price?
faq.answer: We can tell you whether the offer describes the right tract, whether the interest it credits you with matches what the record shows, and which of the terms will matter most over the life of the agreement. What we do not do is put a value on your minerals or tell you whether to sign. That decision is yours, often with your attorney, and our job is to make sure you are making it against an accurate picture of what you actually own.

faq.question: How long does this take?
faq.answer: It depends on the county and on how far back the chain has to be run. Some counties have everything indexed and searchable online. Others mean a day at the courthouse and records filed under a name spelled three different ways. Once we know the tract and the county we can give you a realistic estimate, and we would rather do that at the start than halfway through.

faq.question: What will it cost?
faq.answer: It depends on the scope: how many tracts are involved, how far back the title has to be run, and whether you need a written report you can hand to someone else or an informal read on what you are looking at. Send us the details and we will tell you what the work involves and what it costs before any of it starts.

faq.question: What do you need from me to get started?
faq.answer: Whatever you already have. The offer or division order if you were sent one, any deeds, wills or probate paperwork sitting in a drawer, and the county and state the property is in. If all you have is a letter and a rough idea of where the land is, that is still enough for a first conversation.

pennsylvania_note: In Pennsylvania the surface and the minerals are often owned separately, and severed oil, gas, and coal estates are common. Deeds and oil and gas leases are recorded with the county Recorder of Deeds, and a decedent's estate is handled through the county Register of Wills and the Orphans' Court. Under the Dunham Rule, reaffirmed in Butler v. Charles Powers Estate (2013), a deed that reserves "minerals" does not by itself include oil and gas unless the instrument says so. Pennsylvania has no general forced pooling for the Marcellus, and the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act (58 P.S. section 33.3) requires an oil and gas lease to guarantee the owner at least a one-eighth royalty. This is what the record commonly shows, not legal advice.
conflict_note: We also acquire leases for operators. Under the AAPL Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice, which require a land professional to disclose any interest that may conflict with a client, we will not review your offer on a tract where we are already working for the other side, and we will tell you up front if that is the case.
disclaimer: We are not attorneys and we do not give legal advice. Our work is research and reporting on what the public record shows. Many owners bring their own attorney in for the legal questions, and we are used to working alongside one.
